extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners and patent practitioners (applicants, agents, attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining compliance with the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (and pre‑AIA 112, para.1), including how to assess possession, genus/species support, amended/priority claims, examiner findings, and appropriate Office‑action handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description as proof of possession
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the specification shows that applicant was in possession of the claimed invention is a factual determination reached by considering a number of factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include level of skill and knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical and/or chemical properties, functional characteristics alone or coupled with a known or disclosed correlation between structure and function, and the method of making the claimed invention. Disclosure of any combination of such identifying characteristics that distinguish the claimed invention from other materials and would lead one of skill in the art to the conclusion that the applicant was in possession of the claimed species is sufficient. (See Eli Lilly, Capon v. Eshhar, and related cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Varying sufficiency depending on nature of the art
rubrics_metrics.description: The description needed to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112 varies with the nature and scope of the invention at issue, and with the scientific and technologic knowledge already in existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In mature technologies where the art is well developed, written description issues are less likely for originally filed claims even if the spec discloses only method of making and function. In emerging or unpredictable technologies more evidence is required to show possession; mere method and function may not support product claims. (Cite: Eli Lilly, Amgen, Fiers, Burroughs Wellcome.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Product‑by‑process disclosure limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of only a method of making the invention and the function may not be sufficient to support a product claim other than a product‑by‑process claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the process has actually been used to produce the product, a product‑by‑process claim's written description requirement is clearly satisfied; however, if it's not clear the acts can be performed or the product produced by that process, the requirement may not be satisfied. (See Fiers v. Revel; Amgen.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial structural disclosure may be insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of a partial structure without additional characterization of the product may not be sufficient to evidence possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., in biotechnology, conceiving a gene requires ability to define it to distinguish it from other materials and describe how to obtain it; defining solely by principal biological property is insufficient. Reduction to practice helps corroborate conception and possession. (See Amgen and Burroughs Wellcome.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus support via representative species or identifying characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: The written description requirement for a claimed genus may be satisfied through sufficient description of a representative number of species, reduction to drawings, or by disclosure of relevant identifying characteristics (structure, properties, or function coupled with a known/disclosed structure‑function correlation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'representative number of species' must reflect variation within the genus. Where substantial variation exists, describe a sufficient variety of species. One species may suffice only if the disclosure indicates the patentee invented species sufficient to constitute the genus. (Cites: Eli Lilly, AbbVie, Enzo Biochem, Noelle v. Lederman.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative number concept and unpredictability
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether disclosed species are representative depends on whether one of skill would recognize that the applicant possessed the common attributes of the genus; in unpredictable arts, one species usually will not support a broad genus claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If representative species are not disclosed, the genus claim must be rejected for inadequate written description. In unpredictable arts, the disclosure must adequately reflect structural diversity or establish a reasonable structure‑function correlation. (Cite: AbbVie, Eli Lilly.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure‑function correlation as alternative to enumerating species
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable structure‑function correlation, established in the specification or known in the art, can support a genus claim without listing many species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correlations may be inventor‑described or known at filing. Example: disclosure of an amino acid sequence may sufficiently convey possession of nucleic acids encoding it because the genetic code is known. (See discussion citing In re Bell and In re Baird.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner initial burden to justify written description rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner has the initial burden of presenting evidence or reasoning to explain why persons skilled in the art would not recognize in the original disclosure a description of the invention defined by the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A description as filed is presumed adequate unless the examiner rebuts the presumption with a reasonable basis. The examiner must identify the claim limitation at issue and establish a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art would not recognize possession in view of the disclosure. A general allegation of 'unpredictability in the art' is insufficient. (See Wertheim.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that claim limitations be supported in the original disclosure for priority/benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: To be entitled to an earlier priority or filing date under 35 U.S.C. 119/120/365/386, each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an explicit limitation is not present in the written description whose benefit is sought, it must be shown that a person of ordinary skill would have understood at filing that the description requires that limitation. (Cite: Hyatt v. Boone; In re Wright.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Inherency requires that the missing descriptive matter be necessarily present in the thing described and recognized by persons of ordinary skill; probabilities or possibilities are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extrinsic evidence must make clear that the missing descriptive matter is necessarily present; inherency may not be established by mere possibilities. (See In re Robertson and related discussion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements described as essential must be claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim must include all elements which applicant has described as essential or critical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an element described as essential is not claimed, a new or amended claim must be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre‑AIA 112, para.1) as lacking adequate written description. (Cites: Johnson Worldwide Assoc. v. Zebco; Gentry Gallery; Tronzo v. Biomet.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences when original disclosure lacks support
rubrics_metrics.description: If the originally filed disclosure does not provide support for each claim limitation, or if an essential element is omitted, the claim must be rejected or priority/benefit denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre‑AIA 112, para.1) or denial of the priority/benefit claim is appropriate when support is lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete patentability determination and clear Office action communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must complete the patentability determination under all relevant statutory provisions (35 U.S.C. 101, 112, 102, 103) and clearly communicate findings, conclusions, and their bases in the Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After analyzing the claimed invention under all statutes and reviewing proposed rejections for correctness, only then should any rejection be imposed. The Office action should, when possible, offer helpful suggestions on how to overcome rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling applicant reply and repeat rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon reply by applicant, the examiner must re‑determine patentability in view of the whole record before repeating any written description rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the whole record demonstrates the requirement is satisfied, the examiner should not repeat the rejection in the next Office action. If not, repeat the rejection, fully respond to rebuttal arguments, and properly treat any further showings (including affidavits) submitted in reply. (See In re Alton.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of showing possession (permissible descriptive means)
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession may be shown by describing the claimed invention with all limitations using words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas, reduction to practice, drawings, structural chemical formulas, or by describing distinguishing identifying characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: actual reduction to practice; disclosure that invention was 'ready for patenting' (drawings or structural formulas); distinguishing characteristics sufficient to show applicant was in possession. (Cites: Lockwood; Pfaff; Eli Lilly; Amgen.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject matter need not be described verbatim but must be reasonably conveyed
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject matter of the claim need not be described literally (in haec verba) to satisfy the description requirement, but the disclosure must reasonably convey possession of the later claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim is amended to include subject matter or terminology not present in the application as filed (departure/addition/deletion), the examiner should conclude the claimed subject matter is not described and reject accordingly. (See Vas‑Cath, In re Gosteli, and related discussion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical circumstances raising description issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Written description issues commonly arise in amendments affecting claims, reliance on parent/priority filing dates, interferences, and when an original claim is not sufficiently described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific examples: (I) amendments to claims or spec must be supported (In re Wright); (II) reliance on 35 U.S.C. 120 requires disclosure in parent application; (III) priority under 35 U.S.C. 119 requires corresponding support in foreign/provisional; (IV) claims corresponding to a count in an interference must be supported; (V) original claims may lack support when defined functionally without how function is performed, or when a broad genus is claimed but spec describes only a narrow species. (Cited cases throughout.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner should suggest claim amendments when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: When appropriate, the examiner should suggest amendments to the claims which can be supported by the application's written description, mindful of prohibition against adding new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggest amendments that align with the disclosure but avoid introducing new matter. See Rasmussen for caution about adding new matter to claims or specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of adequacy and standard objective test
rubrics_metrics.description: A description as filed is presumed adequate unless sufficient evidence or reasoning rebuts that presumption; the objective test is whether the description clearly allows persons of ordinary skill in the art to recognize that the inventor invented what is now claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Marzocchi for presumption, In re Gosteli and Vas‑Cath for objective standard: the specification must convey with reasonable clarity to skilled artisans that, as of the filing date, the applicant was in possession of the invention as now claimed.
